title: Metzora: cedar and hyssop (Leviticus 14:4)
hookLine: the tall cedar and the low hyssop; Rashi reads them as pride brought low

cards: Some objects are chosen for what they mean as much as for what they do. A wedding ring is just a circle of metal, until it isn't.
When the priest goes out to the person who may be healed, he asks for a strange little bundle: two living birds, a piece of cedar wood, some scarlet thread, and a sprig of hyssop.
The Torah lists them without a word of explanation. So readers, from the ancient rabbis on, have kept asking: why these four?

teach.b: Start with the two plants. In the Bible the cedar is the great tree of Lebanon: Solomon built the Temple and his palace with its wood. Hyssop is the opposite, a small, low herb growing out of cracks in walls.
The book of Kings, describing Solomon's wisdom, says he spoke of trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop on the wall. Top to bottom, the whole range.
Then Rashi. He starts from the rabbis' teaching that afflictions came because of arrogance and harmful speech. So the cedar stands for the haughtiness that brought the trouble.
And the cure? Let the person lower themselves from their pride, like the worm and like the hyssop.
The worm is the scarlet thread: in Hebrew it's called the worm's scarlet, because the red dye came from a tiny insect. So the bundle holds one very tall thing and two very low ones.
In this reading, the way back into the camp runs downward. Not into shame: Rashi doesn't tell the person to hate themselves. Just smaller, closer to the ground.
The person who once looked down on others comes home by remembering they're a creature among creatures.
Some teachers also note that the cedar stays in the bundle. Nobody throws it out. Height isn't the problem.

how: Jewish teachers often read the purification rites of Metzora as lessons in humility, following Rashi, and the portion is read in synagogue in the spring, often together with Tazria.

p: the low herb on the wall

s: the Torah explains why cedar and hyssop are used
it lists them without explanation. Rashi's reading came much later.
Kings says Solomon spoke of trees from the cedar to the hyssop
the cedar to the hyssop: the whole range.
the scarlet thread was dyed with a plant
the dye came from a tiny insect; Hebrew calls it the worm's scarlet.

games.q: you're Rashi, reading the list: cedar, scarlet, hyssop. the rabbis say the affliction came from arrogance. what do you see?
o: pride, and the way down from it.
games.why: Rashi reads the cedar as haughtiness, and the worm and hyssop as the cure: lower yourself from your pride.

practice: Think of a place where you've been standing a little tall lately: an argument you needed to win, a room where you're quietly sure you're the smartest, a person you talk down to without meaning to.
Picture yourself not falling, just stepping down one notch, eye to eye with them. Notice what you'd say differently from there.

wordCard.voice: Metzora. The portion where the way home is carried in a bundle of cedar, scarlet and hyssop: the tall brought low.

orig.note: Hebrew: "cedar and hyssop": the tall tree and the low herb of Leviticus 14:4.

carryVoice: Your line: from cedar to hyssop. The tall and the low ride home in one bundle. See you tomorrow.
